channel.title: Acme: Daily Reading List
channel.description: Noteworthy articles from across the web.

item.title: WordPress 7.2 reaches full PHP 8.6 compatibility
item.description: WordPress core contributors say every known PHP 8.6 compatibility issue is resolved in WordPress 7.2 Beta 5. The developer note explains the fixes and flags changes plugin and theme authors should test, including font MIME detection, image handling and deprecated functions.

item.title: How two world wars made Jacksonville a Navy town
item.description: Jacksonville History Center CEO Alan Bliss connects the city’s wartime shipbuilding booms to its modern identity. World War I drove industrial growth and migration; World War II cemented the military presence that now includes Mayport, NAS Jacksonville and nearby Kings Bay.

item.title: A practical guide to 2.5 million pages of vintage media history
item.description: This guide maps the Media History Digital Library’s free collection of more than 2.5 million digitized pages from film, broadcasting and recorded-sound trade papers, fan magazines and yearbooks. It explains Lantern full-text search, copyright context and the best collections for research.

item.title: Copyright Office finishes digitizing 25,238 historical record books
item.description: The U.S. Copyright Office has completed digitization of 25,238 bound record books containing more than 21.7 million images of registrations and other filings from 1870 through 1977. The collection is already browsable online, with plans to make individual records easier to search through the Copyright Public Records System.

item.title: SPSFC 6 entry window closes November 29
item.description: The sixth Self-Published Science Fiction Competition is accepting new entries and eligible resubmissions through November 29. Qualifying novels must be self-published science fiction of at least 40,000 words and released by December 7. Judge teams will be finalized in early December, with the winner scheduled for October 2027.

item.title: A fresh census finds RSS still widespread across major sites
item.description: Feeder reports that 942 of the 1,000 most-followed websites it checked still publish working RSS feeds. The survey also notes where support has disappeared and explains how podcasts, WordPress, YouTube and Mastodon continue to generate feeds even when sites hide the familiar orange icon.

item.title: The odd hotel-room origins of fantasy football
item.description: The Pro Football Hall of Fame traces fantasy football to an October 1962 Raiders road trip, when Bill Winkenbach, Bill Tunnell and Scotty Stirling sketched rules in a Manhattan hotel. The first GOPPPL draft followed in August 1963, with George Blanda as the first selection; a public league arrived in 1969.

item.title: Inside the Jacksonville History Center’s 2,000-foot archive
item.description: Jacksonville’s historical archive holds more than 2,000 linear feet of letters, manuscripts and ephemera, plus over 100,000 photographs and negatives, maps, films, books and artifacts. Archivist Erin Mustard explains how preservation storage and catalog descriptions keep 200 years of local records usable for researchers.

item.title: ServiceNow’s module system brings imports, TypeScript and npm dependencies to scoped apps
item.description: ServiceNow’s Zurich documentation explains how scoped applications can organize reusable JavaScript or TypeScript modules with named and default exports, import server APIs explicitly, and declare third-party packages in package.json. It also documents important limits: no global apps, Node.js APIs or undeclared cross-scope access.

item.title: Tracing Lovecraft’s one-week stay in New Orleans
item.description: This compact research note reconstructs H.P. Lovecraft’s June 1932 week in New Orleans with fellow Weird Tales writer E. Hoffmann Price. It identifies Price’s apartment at 305 Royal Street, Lovecraft’s inexpensive St. Charles Street hotel, their long conversations and the surviving memoir and correspondence that document the visit.

item.title: How Poydras Market shaped a lost New Orleans neighborhood
item.description: Before parking lots hollowed out the blocks above Lafayette Square, the bustling Poydras Market supported restaurants, shops, saloons, stables and industry for nearly a century. This illustrated history connects the market’s vanished commercial ecosystem to the modern South Market District and includes an 1864–65 photograph.
item.source: Preservation Resource Center of New Orleans

item.title: What ServiceNow Zurich’s modern JavaScript engine actually supports
item.description: ServiceNow’s Zurich documentation explains where server-side scripts can use ECMAScript 2021 features such as optional chaining, destructuring, const, let and arrow functions. It also distinguishes modern, ES5 Standards and Compatibility modes—useful when upgrading scoped applications without unexpectedly changing older script behavior.

item.title: Why library ebooks can have waiting lists
item.description: OverDrive’s concise explanation of digital lending answers a deceptively thorny question: libraries buy individual ebook or audiobook copies, and most publisher licenses permit only one borrower per copy at a time. Collection budgets determine how many copies are available, so a file that is easy to duplicate can still produce a long hold queue.

item.title: A sourced field guide to what enters the public domain in 2027
item.description: Commons Cut’s living guide tracks U.S. works expected to enter the public domain on January 1, 2027: publications from 1931 and sound recordings from 1926. It usefully flags renewal, foreign-work and version-specific complications, while linking its claims to catalogs and other evidence for deeper copyright archaeology.

item.title: MIT built a full calculus course for independent learners
item.description: MIT’s OpenCourseWare Scholar project turned Calculus I into a self-contained course for people studying outside a classroom. It supplies lectures, recitations, worked examples, problem sets and exams, assumes high-school algebra and trigonometry, and estimates about 150 hours of work—a serious, free route back into mathematics.
